cls: Opioid analgesic - mixed agonist-antagonist (kappa agonist, mu partial agonist/antagonist)
quick: Oral (with naloxone combo): 1 tablet (50 mg pentazocine) every 3-4 h PRN, may increase to 2 tablets; max 12 tablets/day. Parenteral (lactate, non-US): 30 mg IM/SC/IV every 3-4 h
Oral tablets may be taken with or without food
Avoid; prolonged use causes neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS). Animal data show fetal harm
Use with caution; opioids pass into milk and may sedate infant
Caution; substantially renally excreted - reduce dose and monitor in impairment
Caution; reduced hepatic metabolism may accentuate side effects - reduce dose
Avoid - additive CNS/respiratory depression, profound sedation, coma, death
Respiratory rate, sedation, BP, signs of dependence/abuse. HABIT FORMING - Schedule IV controlled substance; monitor for misuse and withdrawal
summary: Pentazocine is a mixed opioid agonist-antagonist (kappa agonist, mu partial agonist/antagonist) used for moderate to severe pain requiring an opioid analgesic when alternatives are inadequate. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance and is habit forming, carrying opioid-class risks of respiratory depression, profound sedation with alcohol/benzodiazepines, abuse, dependence, and withdrawal. The FDA-labeled oral product combines pentazocine with naloxone (to deter parenteral abuse); a parenteral lactate injection (30 mg) is available outside the US. Higher doses can cause psychotomimetic (dysphoric, hallucinatory) effects.
indications: Management of pain severe enough to require an opioid analgesic and for which alternative treatments are inadequate
Moderate to severe acute pain (parenteral, non-US)
Obstetric analgesia and pre-anesthetic medication (parenteral, where approved)

dosage.d: 1 tablet (50 mg pentazocine + 0.5 mg naloxone) every 3-4 hours PRN
dosage.n: Use lowest effective dose for shortest duration; titrate to response

dosage.d: May increase to 2 tablets when needed; total daily dose must not exceed 12 tablets
dosage.n: Reserve higher doses for inadequate response when benefits outweigh risks

dosage.d: 30 mg every 3-4 hours; single doses >30 mg IV or >60 mg IM/SC not recommended
dosage.n: Source: non-US/India parenteral labeling, not the US FDA oral label. Max ~360 mg/day. Avoid repeated SC injection (tissue damage)

dosage.d: Start at low end of dosing range; titrate slowly
dosage.n: Greater sensitivity; higher risk of respiratory depression and reduced hepatic/renal/cardiac function
Safety and effectiveness in patients below 12 years not established (oral label)

admin: Prescribe only by clinicians knowledgeable about opioid use and risk mitigation; use lowest effective dose for shortest duration
Oral tablets may be taken with or without food
Parenteral: aspirate before IM/SC injection to avoid intra-arterial/intravenous misadministration; rotate injection sites and avoid repeated SC use
Reassess regularly for analgesia, adverse effects, and signs of misuse, abuse, or addiction
Consider co-prescribing an opioid overdose reversal agent (naloxone/nalmefene) when overdose risk factors are present
Do not stop abruptly after prolonged use - taper to avoid withdrawal
moa: Pentazocine is a mixed agonist-antagonist at opioid receptors: a partial agonist at the mu receptor and an agonist at the kappa receptor, with weak mu-antagonist activity. Kappa agonism mediates spinal analgesia, sedation, and (at higher doses) psychotomimetic/dysphoric effects. It produces respiratory depression by direct action on brainstem respiratory centers, causes miosis, reduces GI motility (constipation), and may raise blood pressure via catecholamine release. As a mu partial agonist/antagonist it can precipitate withdrawal in patients dependent on full mu agonists.

absolute: Acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or without resuscitative equipment
Known or suspected GI obstruction, including paralytic ileus
Hypersensitivity to pentazocine, naloxone, or formulation excipients (e.g., anaphylaxis)
relative: History of substance use disorder, drug/alcohol abuse, or addiction (habit-forming, Schedule IV - high abuse/dependence potential)
Concurrent benzodiazepines, other CNS depressants, or alcohol
Patients dependent on full mu-opioid agonists (may precipitate withdrawal)
Cardiovascular disease / acute MI (can raise BP via catecholamine release)
Head injury or raised intracranial pressure
monitor: Respiratory rate and depth, especially at initiation and dose increases
Level of sedation and mental status (psychotomimetic effects at higher doses)
Signs of misuse, abuse, addiction, and withdrawal

preg: Avoid in pregnancy. Prolonged use of opioid analgesics during pregnancy can cause neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS), which may be life-threatening; ensure neonatology management is available at delivery. Animal reproduction studies showed neural tube defects (hamster) and increased resorptions/extra ribs (rat). No adequate human data. Use only if clearly needed and counsel on fetal risk.
lact: Use with caution. Opioids are excreted into breast milk and may cause sedation and respiratory depression in the breastfed infant; monitor the infant for drowsiness, feeding difficulty, and breathing problems if used.
renal: Pentazocine (and naloxone) is substantially excreted by the kidney; risk of adverse reactions is greater in renal impairment. Administer with caution, use lower doses, and monitor closely - particularly in the elderly.
hepatic: Decreased hepatic metabolism in extensive liver disease may accentuate side effects (sedation, respiratory depression). Use with caution and consider dose reduction in hepatic impairment.

major: Benzodiazepines and other CNS depressants (alcohol, sedative-hypnotics, anxiolytics, muscle relaxants, general anesthetics, antipsychotics, other opioids) - profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death (boxed warning)
Alcohol - additive CNS and respiratory depression; avoid
Other mixed agonist-antagonist / partial agonist opioids (butorphanol, nalbuphine, buprenorphine) - reduced analgesia and/or precipitated withdrawal; avoid concomitant use
MAO inhibitors (including linezolid, IV methylene blue; current or within 14 days) - CNS excitation and hypertension via catecholamine effects
Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, MAOIs, others) - serotonin syndrome
moderate: Skeletal muscle relaxants - enhanced neuromuscular blockade and increased respiratory depression
Anticholinergic drugs - increased urinary retention and severe constipation / paralytic ileus
minor: Tobacco smoking - enhances metabolic clearance of pentazocine, may reduce effectiveness of a standard dose
interactions.food: No clinically significant food interaction with the oral tablet
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive and potentially fatal CNS and respiratory depression, profound sedation, and coma
interactions.diagnostics: May cause moderate transient eosinophilia and depression of white cells (rarely agranulocytosis); transient elevations in serum amylase

serious: Hallucinations, disorientation, confusion (psychotomimetic effects, esp. >60 mg)
Hypertension or hypotension, circulatory depression, syncope
Serotonin syndrome; adrenal insufficiency; opioid-induced esophageal dysfunction
rare: Erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis
Tissue damage / fibrosis with repeated SC injection (parenteral)
emergency: Coma / circulatory failure (especially with alcohol or other CNS depressants)

monitoring: Respiratory rate, oxygenation, and sedation level - especially at initiation and dose increases
Blood pressure (may rise via catecholamine release)
Signs of misuse, abuse, addiction, and opioid withdrawal (Schedule IV - habit forming)
Renal and hepatic function in at-risk patients
counsel: This medicine is habit forming and can cause dependence and addiction - take exactly as prescribed and do not increase the dose on your own
Do NOT drink alcohol or take benzodiazepines/sedatives with this drug - the combination can be fatal
May cause drowsiness, dizziness, or confusion - do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you
Store securely out of reach of children; accidental ingestion of even one tablet can be fatal to a child
Do not share this medicine; dispose of unused medicine properly
Do not stop suddenly after prolonged use - this can cause withdrawal; ask your doctor about tapering
Seek emergency help (call emergency services) for slowed or difficult breathing, extreme drowsiness, or unresponsiveness
pk: Parenteral: ~15-30 min (IM/SC), 2-3 min IV. Oral: ~15-30 min
Oral peak analgesia ~1-3 hours after dose
Approximately 2-3 hours (prolonged in hepatic or renal impairment)
Analgesia approximately 3-4 hours; requires repeat dosing every 3-4 h
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F). Tablets: tight, light-resistant container; store securely and dispose of properly
pearls: Habit forming: Yes - Schedule IV controlled substance (opioid agonist-antagonist); risk of dependence and withdrawal
As a mu partial agonist/antagonist, pentazocine can precipitate acute withdrawal in patients physically dependent on full mu-opioid agonists (e.g., morphine) - avoid combining
Higher doses (>60 mg) cause psychotomimetic effects - anxiety, nightmares, dysphoria, hallucinations - which limit dose escalation and abuse

The oral formulation combines pentazocine with naloxone (inactive orally) to deter parenteral misuse; naloxone may need larger-than-usual doses to reverse a pentazocine overdose because of its agonist-antagonist nature
Tobacco smoking increases pentazocine clearance and may reduce efficacy; pentazocine can raise blood pressure - use caution in acute MI
Co-prescribe an opioid overdose reversal agent when overdose risk factors are present
missed: If used on a scheduled basis, take the missed dose as soon as remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it - do not double up. As pentazocine is usually taken as needed for pain, simply take the next dose when pain returns and dosing interval allows.
overdose: Overdose causes respiratory depression, somnolence progressing to stupor or coma, skeletal muscle flaccidity, cold/clammy skin, constricted pupils (or mydriasis with hypoxia), bradycardia, hypotension, hypoglycemia, pulmonary edema, seizures, and death; psychotomimetic effects (anxiety, hallucinations) may occur. Manage by securing the airway and assisted ventilation, plus supportive measures (oxygen, vasopressors). Give an opioid reversal agent (naloxone or nalmefene); because pentazocine is a mixed agonist-antagonist, larger-than-usual naloxone doses may be required. In opioid-dependent patients, titrate the antagonist carefully with smaller doses to avoid precipitating severe withdrawal.
